verses.text: Listen to this word, you cows of Bashan, who are on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the poor, who crush the needy, who tell their husbands, “Bring us drinks!”
The Lord Yahweh has sworn by his holiness that behold, “The days shall come on you that they will take you away with hooks, and the last of you with fish hooks.
You will go out at the breaks in the wall, everyone straight before her; and you will cast yourselves into Harmon,” says Yahweh.
“Go to Bethel, and sin; to Gilgal, and sin more. Bring your sacrifices every morning, your tithes every three days,
offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving of that which is leavened, and proclaim free will offerings and brag about them: for this pleases you, you children of Israel,” says the Lord Yahweh.
“I also have given you cleanness of teeth in all your cities, and lack of bread in every town; yet you haven’t returned to me,” says Yahweh.

“I also have withheld the rain from you, when there were yet three months to the harvest; and I caused it to rain on one city, and caused it not to rain on another city. One place was rained on, and the piece where it didn’t rain withered.
So two or three cities staggered to one city to drink water, and were not satisfied: yet you haven’t returned to me,” says Yahweh.

“I struck you with blight and mildew many times in your gardens and your vineyards; and your fig trees and your olive trees have the swarming locust devoured: yet you haven’t returned to me,” says Yahweh.

“I sent plagues among you like I did Egypt. I have slain your young men with the sword, and have carried away your horses; and I filled your nostrils with the stench of your camp, yet you haven’t returned to me,” says Yahweh.
“I have overthrown some of you, as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you were like a burning stick plucked out of the fire; yet you haven’t returned to me,” says Yahweh.
“Therefore thus will I do to you, Israel; because I will do this to you, prepare to meet your God, Israel.

For, behold, he who forms the mountains, and creates the wind, and declares to man what is his thought; who makes the morning darkness, and treads on the high places of the earth: Yahweh, the God of Armies, is his name.”

footnotes.content: Amos speaks directly to the comfortable wives of Samaria—the capital city where wealth had coaxed people away from justice. 'Cows of Bashan' was no compliment; it meant fat and placid, forgetting the hungry at their gate. The Lord notices when comfort becomes cruelty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The image of being led away 'with hooks' paints a hard picture, yet it springs from His holiness—His hatred of injustice. He swears by His own name because He will not let wickedness have the last word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They will flee through breaks in their own walls, each woman running straight ahead with no one to lead or help. Abandonment follows arrogance. Yet even exile speaks His merciful intent: He breaks chains, even if we run.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bethel and Gilgal were shrines where Israel came to worship, yet Amos's tone cuts sharp: 'Go to Bethel and sin.' He means they've turned worship into a machine for self-righteousness, unmoored from the justice the Lord demands. Ritual without repentance is sin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They bring leavened offerings and brag about their free will gifts to an audience of worshipers—performing piety rather than practicing it. The Lord reads the heart beneath each gesture. He watches whether we give to honor Him or to honor ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hunger in their cities—teeth scrubbed clean because there's nothing to eat—was a voice calling them home. Each hardship was a door left open; He kept knocking. Yet 'you haven't returned to me' repeats like a grieving refrain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord withheld rain selectively: one city drenched while another's fields shriveled just beyond the border. This wasn't random cruelty but precise teaching—a sign that His hand shapes the seasons and can wake us if we're watching.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three cities converging on one well, desperate for water that never satisfied their thirst—the picture of people running after every false remedy while the true source waits for them to turn. Thirst is a gift when it drives us toward Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Blight and mildew, locusts that devoured the fig and olive trees—the land itself was speaking. Gardens and vineyards, the pride of a farmer's inheritance, were stripped bare. Yet still they did not hear the Lord's voice in their loss.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He 'sent plagues like Egypt'—a phrase that reaches back to the Exodus, when the Lord broke Pharaoh's grip. Now He was speaking the same language of deliverance to Israel: *Turn, or be set free by judgment rather than grace.*
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A burning stick snatched from fire—that's what Israel was, spared yet barely. The image is raw mercy: saved, yet singed, yet still refusing to recognize the hand that pulled them out. Sometimes the narrowest escapes carry the loudest warnings.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo here: when we ignore every gentle knock—hunger, loss, disease, near-escape—comes the blunt call: 'Prepare to meet your God.' It rings still. He gives us every chance to turn before the final meeting arrives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The God who forms mountains and creates wind, who declares human thought and 'makes morning darkness'—an almost terrifying portrait of a power that penetrates everything. He treads the high places. This is the One calling Israel back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
